questions.question_text: Which of the following is true of Huntington disease?

options.text: Genetic defect located on the long arm of chromosome 4
Results from an expanded CGG repeat

questions.explanation:
Huntington disease is a rare neurodegenerative disorder of the central nervous system, with a genetic autosomal dominant inheritance. It results from the expansion of a CAG trinucleotide repeat in the HTT (huntingtin) gene on the short arm of chromosome 4. Onset is usually during the 30s and 40s. There is a small number of juvenile-onset cases. An increased risk of suicide in Huntington disease is well documented, with rates significantly higher than those of the general population as well as other neurodegenerative diseases.
Ref: Bachoud-Lévi AC et al. International Guidelines for the treatment of Huntington’s Disease. Frontiers in neurology. 2019;10:710.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 166.
Kachian ZR et al. Suicidal ideation and behavior in Huntington's disease: Systematic review and recommendations. Journal of a!ective disorders. 2019 May 1;250:319-29.

questions.question_text: In which of the following dementias is recognition memory better than recall memory?
questions.explanation:
HIV-associated dementia is a subcortical dementia. Recall memory is more impaired than recognition memory.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 149.
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 244.

questions.question_text: A 42-year-old man has been experiencing troublesome motor activity for the last three years. He also has symptoms of irritability, anxiety, and low mood. He turns up an hour late for his medical appointment and shouts at the receptionist for not being punctual. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Huntington disease is a rare neurodegenerative disorder of the central nervous system, with a genetic autosomal dominant inheritance. Onset is usually during the 30s and 40s. Worsening chorea is characterised by initial jerks, tics, gross involuntary movements of all parts of the body, grimacing, and dysarthria. Anxiety and depression are common, as is executive dysfunction with impulsivity and aggression.
Ref: Bachoud-Lévi AC et al. International Guidelines for the treatment of Huntington’s Disease. Frontiers in neurology. 2019;10:710.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 166.

questions.question_text: The greatest risk factor for vascular dementia is
questions.explanation:
The greatest risk factors for stroke and white matter hyperintensities and, consequently, for vascular dementia are high systolic and high diastolic blood pressure.
Ref: Van Der Flier WM et al. Vascular cognitive impairment. Nature Reviews Disease Primers. 2018 Feb 15;4(1):1-6.

questions.question_text: Hyperhomocysteinaemia is a modifiable risk factor for
questions.explanation:
Elevated plasma total homocysteine is a modifiable risk factor for the development of cognitive decline, dementia, and Alzheimer disease in older persons.
Ref: Smith AD et al. Homocysteine and dementia: an international consensus statement. Journal of Alzheimer's Disease. 2018 Jan 1;62(2):561-70.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true for very-late-onset schizophrenia-like psychosis?

options.text: Response to treatment is much better than early onset schizophrenia
A strong family history is often noted
There is usually a life long history of poor social and occupational functioning
It is seen more often in females than males

correct_answer.text: It is seen more often in females than males

correct_answers.text: It is seen more often in females than males

questions.explanation:
Compared with early- or late-onset schizophrenia, very-late-onset schizophrenia-like psychosis is characterised by greater likelihood of sensory impairment, social isolation, visual hallucinations, lesser likelihood of formal thought disorder and a!ective blunting, lesser likelihood of family history of schizophrenia, and greater risk of developing tardive dyskinesia. There is a preponderance of women, with an accelerating incidence rate after age 80.
Ref: Tampi RR et al. Psychotic disorders in late life: a narrative review. Therapeutic advances in psychopharmacology. 2019 Oct;9:1-13.
Gautam S et al. Clinical practice guideline for management of psychoses in elderly. Indian journal of psychiatry. 2018 Feb;60(Suppl 3):S363.

questions.question_text: A 57-year-old man has developed Parkinson disease. He starts sending his wife sexually abusive text messages and making sexually o!ensive comments that are out of character for him. Which of the following medications is most likely to have caused this presentation?

options.text: A monoamine oxidase type B inhibitor

questions.explanation:
Impulse control disorders (ICD) are common in patients with Parkinson disease (PD). This can include compulsive gambling, shopping, eating, and hypersexual behaviours. Hypersexual behaviours have been shown to be one the earliest signs of development of ICD in PD. Younger-onset PD, male sex, and a history of behavioural problems are commonly associated with hypersexual behaviours. Several medications used to treat PD have been linked to the development and/or exacerbation of ICD and hypersexual behaviours in these patients. Individually, dopamine agonists and levodopa have been shown to increase hypersexual behaviours in PD patients.
Ref: Sarangi A et al. Treatment and Management of Sexual Disinhibition in Elderly Patients With Neurocognitive Disorders. Cureus. 2021 Oct 3;13(10).
Jones S et al. Neuropsychiatric symptoms in Parkinson's disease: aetiology, diagnosis and treatment. BJPsych Advances. 2020:1-10.

questions.question_text: What is the most common psychological and behavioural symptom in patients with Huntington disease?
questions.explanation:
Apathy is 'a quantifiable reduction in goal-directed behaviour', manifesting clinically as a reduction in interest, spontaneity, motivation, and drive. It is the most frequent psychological and behavioural symptom in Huntington disease (HD), especially in the middle and later stages, causing a severe reduction in activities of daily living. With regard to cognitive and psychological symptoms, apathy and irritability are the two faces of the same coin. A patient can be apathetic in the morning and irritable in the afternoon, depending on the situation. As is the case for irritability, apathy can be caused by environmental and psychological issues. Apathy may also be an adaptive response when the patient feels overwhelmed by too much stimulation (HD patients are more sensitive to noise and environmental interferences), or with the feeling that their disease is progressing.
Ref: Bachoud-Lévi AC et al. International Guidelines for the treatment of Huntington's Disease. Frontiers in neurology. 2019;10:710.

questions.question_text: Deficits on tests of attention and visuospatial ability may be especially prominent in
questions.explanation:
The pattern of cognitive impairment in dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) di!ers from that seen in Alzheimer disease in that short-term memory loss is less prominent (as seen predominantly in Alzheimer disease), but deficits in visuospatial, attention, and executive cognitive domains are more pronounced. Deficits on tests of attention, executive function, and visuospatial ability may be especially prominent and occur early in DLB.
Ref: Sanford AM. Lewy body dementia. Clinics in geriatric medicine. 2018 Nov 1;34(4):603-15.
McKeith IG et al. Diagnosis and management of dementia with Lewy bodies: Fourth consensus report of the DLB Consortium. Neurology. 2017 Jul 4;89(1):88-100.

questions.question_text: A 63-year-old woman with a mixed a!ective state also su!ers from psoriasis. Which drug is most likely to worsen her skin condition?
questions.explanation:
Some skin conditions such as psoriasis and acne can be aggravated by lithium therapy.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 250.

questions.question_text: A 74-year-old man presents with a history of forgetfulness and some confusion at times. Which of the following factors is protective against the development of dementia?
questions.explanation:
There is an association between lower educational levels and a higher incidence of dementia and Alzheimer disease. The cognitive reserve hypothesis suggests that education and intellectual stimulation extend neural reserve. Therefore, the brain can withstand more insults before developing clinical symptoms of dementia.
Ref: Lilford P, Hughes JC. Epidemiology and mental illness in old age. BJPsych Advances. 2020 Mar;26(2):92-103.

questions.question_text: Which of the following interventions is not recommended when managing delirium in the elderly?

options.text: Achieve optimal levels of environmental stimulation
Preferably use low dose haloperidol for patients who require drug treatment
Ensure the safety of all patients and their immediate surroundings
Preferably use benzodiazepines for patients who require drug treatment

correct_answer.text: Preferably use benzodiazepines for patients who require drug treatment

correct_answers.text: Preferably use benzodiazepines for patients who require drug treatment

questions.explanation:
When managing delirium, it should be ensured that the environment is safe. Optimise stimulation by ensuring adequate lighting, reducing unnecessary noise, mobilising the patient when possible, and correcting any sensory impairment (e.g. hearing aids, glasses). Psychotropic medication should be used with caution in delirium and only for situations that have not yielded to non-pharmacological interventions. Conventionally, the antipsychotic of choice is haloperidol, given its absence of anticholinergic side e!ects. The use of antipsychotics is controversial, and there is little evidence to indicate that they should be used to treat delirium directly. There is no evidence to support the use of benzodiazepines in managing delirium not associated with alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 855.
FitzGerald JM, Price A. Delirium in the acute hospital setting: the role of psychiatry. BJPsych Advances. 2020 Jul 30:1-11.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about anxiety disorders in late life is correct?

options.text: Social anxiety disorder and panic disorder predominate
Anxiety content is usually from early life experiences
The estimated prevalence of anxiety disorders is 20-30%
Women are more commonly a!ected than men
Specific phobia and generalised anxiety disorder are uncommon

correct_answer.text: Women are more commonly a!ected than men

correct_answers.text: Women are more commonly a!ected than men

questions.explanation:
The estimated prevalence of anxiety disorders in older adults is 4-14%. They are more common among women than men. Specific phobia is the most prevalent anxiety disorder among older adults; fear of falling is most common. Generalised anxiety disorder is one of the most common anxiety disorders in older adults; anxiety content reflects multiple issues that arise in later stages of life (e.g. health, welfare or loss of loved ones, life transitions, retirement, caregiving responsibilities), and economic and legal issues (e.g. reduced income, increased health care costs, end-of-life planning). Onset of social anxiety disorder is typically not in late life. Panic disorder is relatively infrequent in older adults and onset is typically in younger adulthood.
Ref: Ramos K, Stanley MA. Anxiety disorders in late life. Psychiatric Clinics. 2018 Mar 1;41(1):55-64.

questions.question_text: Which of the following neuroimaging techniques that may be used when assessing dementia is helpful in studying white matter lesions and vascular lesions?
questions.explanation:
MRI scans are useful in examining for neoplasms, vascular malformations, seizure foci, demyelinating disorders, neurodegenerative disorders, and infarctions. MRI better discriminates the interface between grey and white matter and is useful in detecting a variety of white matter lesions in the periventricular and subcortical regions. White matter abnormalities are detected in older patients with hypertension, vascular dementia, and dementia of the Alzheimer type.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 226.

questions.question_text: A 70-year-old man has been diagnosed with Lewy body dementia. He is being started on rivastigmine. Which of the following side effects is most likely to occur?
questions.explanation:
The most common side effects of rivastigmine are anorexia, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhoea.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 605.

questions.question_text: The most common psychiatric side effect of levo-dopa among the following is
questions.explanation: Up to 1/3rd of patients complain of psychiatric side effects when taking levodopa therapy. Nearly 30% of those taking levodopa complain of nightmares and vivid dreams. This is followed by 7% with night terrors, 5% with delirium and 3% with delusional disorder.

questions.question_text: The neurotransmitters most often implicated in the pathophysiology of Alzheimer disease are
questions.explanation:
The neurotransmitters usually implicated in the pathophysiologic condition of Alzheimer disease (AD) are acetylcholine and norepinephrine, both of which are likely hypoactive in AD. Under normal circumstances, neurons in the basal nucleus of Meynert synthesise acetylcholine (ACh) and send axonal projections throughout the entire cerebral cortex and the limbic system to provide cholinergic innervation. Loss of neurons in the basal nucleus of Meynert characterises AD. As with the distribution of the macroscopic and microscopic changes in AD, ACh activity is particularly reduced in the cortical association areas and limbic system. AD is also associated with reduced concentrations of other established or putative neurotransmitters: somatostatin, substance P, norepinephrine (noradrenaline), vasopressin, and several other polypeptides. However, compared to the ACh loss, their concentrations are not decreased profoundly or consistently.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 240.
Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman’s Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9th Edition. 2023. p. 122.

questions.question_text: The personality disorder that is most prevalent in older adults is
questions.explanation:
Personality disorder diagnoses usually seen in late life include the dependent, obsessive-compulsive, histrionic, paranoid, schizoid, and avoidant types. Studies suggest that these diagnoses remain stable over the lifespan or even increase. In several studies, obsessive-compulsive personality disorder has been found to be the most prevalent in older adults. Some studies indicate that borderline personality disorders are less prevalent among older people than among younger people.
Ref: Bangash A. Personality disorders in later life: epidemiology, presentation and management. BJPsych Advances. 2020 Jul;26(4):208-18.
Penders KA et al. Personality disorders in older adults: A review of epidemiology, assessment, and treatment. Current Psychiatry Reports. 2020 Mar;22(3):1-4.

questions.question_text: Which of the following has the most evidence for the treatment of psychosis in patients with dementia?
questions.explanation:
Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) include a wide range of di#culties, including aggression, agitation, vocalisation, distress during care, disinhibition, hallucinations, delusions, apathy, low mood, and anxiety. Typical antipsychotics show no clear e#cacy in BPSD (except for haloperidol), but atypical antipsychotics do have some e#cacy. A Comparative E!ectiveness Review found that the most e!ective antipsychotics include risperidone (psychosis, agitation, overall BPSD), olanzapine (agitation), and aripiprazole (overall BPSD). Though commonly used, quetiapine has failed to show e!ectiveness for BPSD, except at higher doses that may not be well tolerated. A Cochrane review of atypical antipsychotics for aggression and psychosis in Alzheimer dementia concluded that risperidone and olanzapine are useful in diminishing aggression, and risperidone reduces psychotic symptoms.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 644-646.

questions.question_text: In the UK, warnings are currently in place regarding increased mortality and a possible risk of cerebrovascular events in patients with dementia who are prescribed
questions.explanation:
Following analysis of published and unpublished data in 2004, warnings were issued in the UK and USA regarding increased mortality in patients with dementia with certain second-generation antipsychotics (SGAs) – mainly risperidone and olanzapine. These warnings have been extended to include all SGAs as well as conventional antipsychotics, and a warning about a possible risk of cerebrovascular events has now been added to product labelling for all FGAs and SGAs.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 646.

questions.question_text: Delusional content in late-onset schizophrenia and very-late-onset schizophrenia-like psychosis is most likely to be
questions.explanation:
Critical di!erences exist in the clinical presentation of LOS and VLOS compared with the early-onset type. Researchers have generally found a female preponderance, lower genetic risk (reflected by a lower incidence of family history of psychosis), and higher rates of and more severe paranoid symptoms and persecutory delusions in LOS and VLOS patients. Partition delusions – concerning the unwanted permeability of borders - are highly prominent. On the other hand, formal thought disorder is usually absent. Furthermore, there are fewer negative symptoms such as a!ective flattening in LOS and VLOS compared to EOS.
Ref: Suen YN et al. Late-onset psychosis and very-late-onset-schizophrenia-like-psychosis: an updated systematic review. International Review of Psychiatry. 2019 Aug 18;31(5-6):523-42.
Van Assche L et al. The neuropsychology and neurobiology of late-onset schizophrenia and very-late-onset schizophrenia-like psychosis: a critical review. Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews. 2017 Dec 1;83:604-21.

questions.question_text: Factors associated with a better prognosis in Alzheimer disease include
questions.explanation:
Data suggest that in persons with an early onset of dementia or with a family history of dementia, the disease is likely to have a rapid course. Male sex and older age have been associated with increased risk of mortality in Alzheimer dementia (AD). Other predisposing factors for an increased risk of mortality are more severe executive dysfunction, presence of medial temporal lobe atrophy, and higher p-tau in CSF, indicative of more severe AD pathology.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 238.
Rhodius-Meester HF et al. Disease-related determinants are associated with mortality in dementia due to Alzheimer’s disease. Alzheimer's research & therapy. 2018 Dec;10(1):1-10.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a good prognostic factor in late life depression?

options.text: Severe life events during follow up period

questions.explanation: Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 553.

questions.question_text: The response to antidepressants is expected to be generally poor in
questions.explanation: Alexopoulos et al. (1997) proposed that cerebral ischaemic damage to the frontal-subcortical circuits could predispose, precipitate and perpetuate late-onset depression. Simpson et al. studied the association between subcortical disease and antidepressant response in late-life depression, concluding that a poor response could be expected in patients with vascular depression.

questions.question_text: A 76-year-old woman presents to her GP upon her daughter's insistence. She exhibits features of very-late-onset schizophrenia-like psychosis. Which of the following types of delusions is most likely to be seen?
questions.explanation:
Critical di!erences exist in the clinical presentation of LOS and VLOS compared with the early-onset type. Researchers have generally found a female preponderance, lower genetic risk (reflected by a lower incidence of family history of psychosis), and higher rates of and more severe paranoid symptoms and persecutory delusions in LOS and VLOS patients. Partition delusions – concerning the unwanted permeability of borders - are highly prominent.
Ref: Suen YN et al. Late-onset psychosis and very-late-onset-schizophrenia-like-psychosis: an updated systematic review. International Review of Psychiatry. 2019 Aug 18;31(5-6):523-42.
Van Assche L et al. The neuropsychology and neurobiology of late-onset schizophrenia and very-late-onset schizophrenia-like psychosis: a critical review. Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews. 2017 Dec 1;83:604-21.

questions.question_text: The most prevalent anxiety disorder among older adults is
questions.explanation:
The estimated prevalence of anxiety disorders in older adults is 4-14%. They are more common among women than men. Specific phobia is the most prevalent anxiety disorder among older adults; fear of falling is most common. Generalised anxiety disorder is one of the most common anxiety disorders in older adults; anxiety content reflects multiple issues that arise in later stages of life (e.g. health, welfare or loss of loved ones, life transitions, retirement, caregiving responsibilities), and economic and legal issues (e.g. reduced income, increased health care costs, end-of-life planning). Onset of social anxiety disorder is typically not in late life. Panic disorder is relatively infrequent in older adults and onset is typically in younger adulthood.
Ref: Ramos K, Stanley MA. Anxiety disorders in late life. Psychiatric Clinics. 2018 Mar 1;41(1):55-64.

questions.question_text: A 65-year-old man admitted to a neurology unit has an unsteady gait and repeated falls. This is most likely to be associated with
questions.explanation:
Polypharmacy has been repeatedly linked to fall incidence and gait disturbances in older adults.
Ref: Montero-Odasso M et al. Polypharmacy, Gait Performance, and Falls in Community-Dwelling Older Adults. Results from the Gait and Brain Study. Journal of the American Geriatrics Society. 2019 Jun;67(6):1182-8.

questions.question_text: When diagnosing probable Alzheimer Disease dementia according to the NIA-AA criteria, which of the following statements regarding biomarkers is true?

options.text: Biomarkers should be used for routine diagnostic purposes
Biomarkers are well standardised across di!erent locales
Biomarkers are easily accessible in the community
Biomarker evidence may increase diagnostic certainty
NIA-AA criteria make no mention of biomarkers

correct_answer.text: Biomarker evidence may increase diagnostic certainty

correct_answers.text: Biomarker evidence may increase diagnostic certainty

questions.explanation:
In 1984, criteria for the clinical diagnosis of Alzheimer disease (AD) were established by the NINCDS-ADRDA workgroup. More recently, the National Institute on Aging-Alzheimer Association (NIA-AA) group published new criteria for AD dementia that incorporate recent scientific advances. In persons who meet the NIA-AA criteria for probable AD dementia, biomarker evidence may increase the certainty that the basis for the clinical dementia syndrome is the AD pathophysiological process. However, the criteria do not advocate the use of AD biomarker tests for routine diagnostic purposes. It is recognised that there is limited standardisation of biomarkers from one locale to another and that access to biomarkers is limited to varying degrees in the community settings. CSF markers of amyloid and tau may be useful diagnostic markers of AD, but further standardisation and validation is required before they can be more widely used clinically.
Ref: Jack Jr CR, et al. Introduction to revised criteria for the diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease: National Institute on Aging and the Alzheimer Association Workgroups. Alzheimer's & dementia: the journal of the Alzheimer's Association. 2011 May;7(3):257.
McKhann, G.M. et al 2011. The diagnosis of dementia due to Alzheimer's disease: recommendations from the National Institute on Aging-Alzheimer's Association workgroups on diagnostic guidelines for Alzheimer's disease. Alzheimer's & dementia, 7(3), pp.263-269.
O’Brien et al. Clinical practice with anti-dementia drugs: a revised (third) consensus statement from the British Association for Psychopharmacology. Journal of Psychopharmacology. 2017 Feb;31(2):147-68.

questions.question_text: Compared with early-onset depression, older adults with late-onset depression tend to present more often with symptoms of
questions.explanation:
There are no clear distinctions between the clinical presentation of depression in the elderly and that in younger patients. However, some symptoms are often more striking. Severe psychomotor retardation or agitation occurs in up to 30% of depressed elderly patients. Depressive delusions regarding poverty, physical illness, or nihilistic in nature are common. Classic symptoms may not be evident, and the patient may instead present with somatic, anxiety, or hypochondriacal complaints. A high index of suspicion is required when older patients present with these symptoms, especially abnormal illness behaviour.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 552.

questions.question_text: A 75-year-old man with Parkinson disease develops psychosis unrelated to levodopa use. Of those listed, which is the best antipsychotic for his treatment?
questions.explanation:
Clozapine, quetiapine, and pimavanserin have shown some e#cacy in treating psychosis in Parkinson disease. Clozapine has the most robust evidence base. However, its use is limited by agranulocytosis risk and the associated need for blood count monitoring. In clinical practice, quetiapine is more readily used than clozapine, given its side e!ect profile compared to clozapine. Other neuroleptics have thus far demonstrated mixed results with increased risk of extrapyramidal worsening. The introduction of pimavanserin has provided another treatment option for Parkinson disease psychosis, decreasing concern for deterioration in motor function.
Ref: Kyle K, Bronstein JM. Treatment of psychosis in Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy Bodies: A review. Parkinsonism & Related Disorders. 2020 Jun 1;75:55-62.

questions.question_text: Hormone replacement therapy should be prescribed for the
questions.explanation:
As highlighted in the most recent BAP guidelines, hormone replacement therapy (unopposed oestrogen or combined oestrogen and progestin) is not e!ective either in treating cognition in Alzheimer disease, or for the primary prevention of all-cause dementia or Alzheimer disease. There is type I evidence that it is harmful (increases dementia risk). Hormone replacement therapy should NOT be prescribed either as a prevention or treatment for dementia, including Alzheimer disease.
Ref: O’Brien et al. Clinical practice with anti-dementia drugs: a revised (third) consensus statement from the British Association for Psychopharmacology. Journal of Psychopharmacology. 2017 Feb;31(2):147-68.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a neurobiological feature of the normal ageing process?

options.text: Loss of nerve cells in the hippocampus
Reduction in the weight of the brain
Reduction in cerebral blood flow in the frontal lobe

questions.explanation:
Biological changes in the brain associated with ageing include:
-       Decrease in gross brain weight, about 17% by age 80 in both sexes
-       Widened sulci, smaller convolutions, gyral atrophy
-       Ventricles enlarge
-       Increased transport across blood-brain barrier
-       Decreased cerebral blood flow and oxygenation
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 915.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements concerning pharmacokinetics in the elderly is true?

options.text: Renal blood flow decreases with age even in those with normal physical health
Total gastrointestinal drug absorption is reduced
25% of adult renal function is lost by 80 years
Serum creatinine measurement is the most accurate way of measuring renal function

correct_answer.text: Renal blood flow decreases with age even in those with normal physical health

correct_answers.text: Renal blood flow decreases with age even in those with normal physical health

questions.explanation:
How ageing a!ects drug therapy (pharmacokinetics):
-       Gut motility decreases with age, as does gastric acid secretion; drugs are absorbed more slowly but the same amount is absorbed
-       Renal function declines with age; 35% of function is lost by 65 years and 50% by age 80
-       Measurement of serum creatinine can be misleading because muscle mass is reduced, so less creatinine is produced
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 602.

questions.question_text: A70 year old lady has been diagnosed with Alzheimer's dementia recently. What is the risk of same illness for her sister provided there is no other family history of Alzheimer's dementia?

options.text: Risk will be three times higher

correct_answer.text: Risk will be three times higher

correct_answers.text: Risk will be three times higher

questions.explanation: The actual predicted risk of developing Alzheimer's disease in the first-degree relatives of probands with Alzheimer's disease is 15-19%, compared with 5% in controls. Thus, the risk to the first-degree relatives of patients with Alzheimer's disease who developed the disorder at any time up to the age of 85 years is increased some 3 - 4 times relative to the risk in controls. This would seem to translate to a risk of developing Alzheimer's disease of between one in five and one in six. Liddell et al. (2001) Genetic risk of Alzheimer's disease: advising relatives. The British Journal of Psychiatry, 178, 7-11.

questions.question_text: You are seeing a 77-year-old man with late onset psychosis. He has a history of falls due to postural hypotension. Which drug is most likely to cause orthostatic hypotension?
questions.explanation: Risperidone and Clozapine are two drugs, which have a greater risk of causing severe postural hypotension. The suggested drugs are amisulpride, aripiprazole, haloperidol and sulpiride.

questions.question_text: Which of the following drugs has demonstrated benefit in the treatment of hallucinations in dementia with Lewy bodies?
questions.explanation:
Early RCTs of rivastigmine in dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) demonstrated benefit in cognition and neuropsychiatric symptoms including hallucinations, apathy, anxiety, and sleep disorders. Newer data have also demonstrated benefit of donepezil in DLB. Meta-analyses of Class I clinical trials of rivastigmine and donepezil support the use of these medications in DLB for improving cognition, global function, and activities of daily living. Even if patient do not improve with these medications, there is evidence that they are less likely to deteriorate while taking them. The e#cacy of memantine is less clear, but it is well-tolerated and may have benefits as monotherapy or adjunctive to a cholinesterase inhibitor.
Ref: O’Brien et al. Clinical practice with anti-dementia drugs: a revised (third) consensus statement from the British Association for Psychopharmacology. Journal of Psychopharmacology. 2017 Feb;31(2):147-68.
McKeith IG et al. Diagnosis and management of dementia with Lewy bodies: Fourth consensus report of the DLB Consortium. Neurology. 2017 Jul 4;89(1):88-100.

questions.question_text: A 70-year-old gentleman su!ers from Parkinson's disease and is also currently depressed. His wife says he has been sending her sexually explicit texts and also accused her of having an a!air. This is a new type of behaviour and is out of keeping with his previous pattern of behaviour when depressed. Which drug is most likely to account for this presentation?
questions.explanation: Ropinirole can be used by itself or in conjunction with levodopa to treat Parkinson's disease, and is particularly useful in people for whom levodopa alone is no longer providing adequate control of symptom. Ropinirole works by stimulating these same receptor sites. This produces the same e!ects as dopamine and acts as a dopamine substitute. Increased sex drive (libido) and excessive interest or involvement in sexual activity (hypersexuality) is uncommon but possible side e!ect of this medication (Retrieved from [http://www.netdoctor.co.uk/seniors-health/medicines/requip.html](https://www.google.com/search?q=http://www.netdoctor.co.uk/seniors-health/medicines/requip.html)).

questions.question_text: A 72-year-old woman has been calling her family near-daily for the past 6 months to say that she smells gas. She is convinced that her neighbours are trying to poison her by sending gas through the walls. She has called the police on multiple occasions and often stays up all night, convinced that she will die of poisoning if she goes to sleep. Though she is anxious about the situation, her a!ect is otherwise euthymic. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Critical di!erences exist in the clinical presentation of late-onset schizophrenia (LOS) and very-late-onset schizophrenia-like psychosis (VLOS) compared with early-onset schizophrenia. Researchers have generally found a female preponderance, lower genetic risk (reflected by a lower incidence of family history of psychosis), and higher rates of and more severe paranoid symptoms and persecutory delusions in LOS and VLOS patients. Partition delusions – concerning the unwanted permeability of borders - are highly prominent. Both schizophrenia and delusional disorder may be characterised by persistent delusions. If other features are present that meet the diagnostic requirements for schizophrenia (i.e., persistent hallucinations, disorganised thinking, negative symptoms, disorganised or abnormal psychomotor behaviour, or experiences of influence, passivity, or control), a diagnosis of schizophrenia should be made instead of a diagnosis of delusional disorder. However, hallucinations that are consistent with the content of the delusions and do not occur persistently (i.e., with regular frequency for 1 month or longer) are consistent with a diagnosis of delusional disorder rather than schizophrenia.
Ref: Suen YN et al. Late-onset psychosis and very-late-onset-schizophrenia-like-psychosis: an updated systematic review. International Review of Psychiatry. 2019 Aug 18;31(5-6):523-42.
Van Assche L et al. The neuropsychology and neurobiology of late-onset schizophrenia and very-late-onset schizophrenia-like psychosis: a critical review. Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews. 2017 Dec 1;83:604-21.
International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a recognized neuroimaging finding in late-onset depression?

options.text: Reduction in the volume of the caudate nucleus
Reduction in grey matter volume in the frontal and temporal lobes

questions.explanation:
Depression, including late-onset depression, has been repeatedly associated with ventricular enlargement (not shrinkage of the ventricles).
Ref: Zhuo C et al. The rise and fall of MRI studies in major depressive disorder. Translational psychiatry. 2019 Dec 9;9(1):1-4.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following statements about learning and memory in the elderly is not true?

options.text: The elderly take longer than young persons to learn new material
IQ remains stable until approximately 70 years of age
Complete learning of new materials still occurs

questions.explanation:
Simple recall has been repeatedly shown to decline with age.
Ref: Graves LV, Moreno CC, Seewald M, Holden HM, Van Etten EJ, Uttarwar V, McDonald CR, Delano-Wood L, Bondi MW, Woods SP, Delis DC. E!ects of age and gender on recall and recognition discriminability. Archives of Clinical Neuropsychology. 2017 Dec 1;32(8):972-9.

questions.question_text: Which class of antidepressants is generally used as first-line treatment for late-onset depression?
questions.explanation:
A Cochrane review examining the e#cacy, and associated withdrawal rates, of di!erent classes of antidepressants in older people found that SSRIs and tricyclics are of the same e#cacy. However, TCAs are associated with higher withdrawal rates. NICE recommends starting with an SSRI (sertraline is commonly used first line in older people). There is no ideal antidepressant in older people, and all are associated with problems. TCAs are broadly considered less desirable due to the increased risk of cardiac conduction abnormalities and anticholinergic e!ects. SSRIs are generally better tolerated than TCAs; however, they increase the risk of bleeding. Older people are also particularly prone to develop hyponatraemia with SSRIs, as well as postural hypotension and falls.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 673-676.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is not a prion disease?
questions.explanation:
Prion diseases are rare, rapidly progressive dementing illnesses caused by the spread of deposits of abnormal prion protein (PRNP) throughout the brain as a result of either inherited genetic mutation, sporadic mutation, or infection. The typical pathological finding is spongy encephalopathy. Prion diseases include Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, new variant CJD, fatal familial insomnia, Gerstmann-Straussler-Scheinker syndrome, and kuru.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 168.

questions.question_text: Classically, vascular dementia has been distinguished from dementia of the Alzheimer type by
questions.explanation:
Classically, vascular dementia has been distinguished from dementia of Alzheimer type by the decremental (stepwise) deterioration that can accompany cerebrovascular disease over time. Although this discrete, stepwise deterioration may not be apparent in all cases, focal neurological symptoms and standard risk factors for cerebrovascular disease are more common in vascular dementia than dementia of the Alzheimer type.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 236.

options.text: A past history of depression and/or an identifiable precipitant
Onset can be dated with some precision
Don't know answers typical in cognitive tests
Long duration before medical help is sought

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements concerning pharmacokinetics in the elderly is true?

options.text: Older adults have a decreased volume of distribution for some fat-soluble drugs
There is a significant reduction of metabolic capacity of the liver in older adults
Drugs primarily excreted via the kidney will accumulate in the elderly, leading to adverse e!ects
Estimated glomerular filtration rate should not be used as a measure of renal function in the elderly
Older adults have less body fat and more body water than younger adults

correct_answer.text: Drugs primarily excreted via the kidney will accumulate in the elderly, leading to adverse e!ects

correct_answers.text: Drugs primarily excreted via the kidney will accumulate in the elderly, leading to adverse e!ects

questions.explanation:
How ageing a How ageing a!ects drug therapy (pharmacokinetics): ects drug therapy (pharmacokinetics):
-       Older adults have more body fat, less body water, and less albumin than younger adults
-       Older adults have an increased volume of distribution and longer duration of action for some fat-soluble drugs
-       Liver size is reduced in the elderly, but if healthy, there is no significant reduction in metabolic capacity
-       Drugs primarily excreted via the kidney will accumulate in the elderly, leading to toxicity and adverse e!ects
-       Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) should be used as a measure of renal function in the elderly
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 602.

questions.question_text: Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia

options.text: Is also known as Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease
Primarily a!ects the parietal and occipital lobes
Is caused by one known genetic mutation
Has an age of onset from 65-85 years

questions.explanation:
The frontotemporal dementias are a set of overlapping clinical syndromes caused by disease primarily a!ecting the frontal and temporal lobes. 40% have positive family history, 10% due to autosomal dominant mutations (e.g. MAPT, GRN, C9ORF72). Behavioural variant FTD (bvFTD or Pick disease) is the most common subtype. Onset is usually 45-65 years of age. Grossly, the cerebral atrophy in bvFTD, which is often so severe as to be described as ‘knife-edge’ atrophy, is circumscribed and most evident in the frontal lobes. Imaging may be normal or CT/MRI may show bilateral (asymmetrical) abnormalities of the frontal/temporal lobes.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 160.
Gray F, Duyckaerts C, de Girolami U. Escourolle and Poirier’s Manual of Basic Neuropathology, 6th Edition. 2019. p. 192.

questions.question_text: Which of the following features is not reflective of the biological changes seen with the normal aging process?

options.text: Progressive hearing loss particularly at the high frequencies
Cardiac output maintained in the absence of coronary heart disease

questions.explanation:
Biological changes associated with ageing include: Biological changes associated with ageing include:
-       Thickening of the optic lens, reduced peripheral vision
-       High frequency sound hearing loss (presbyacusis) – 25% show loss by age 60, 65% by age 80
-       Decrease in melatonin
-       Impaired T-cell response to antigens
-       Increase in size and weight of heart
-       Decreased elasticity of heart valves
-       Altered homeostasis of blood pressure
-       Cardiac output maintained in the absence of coronary heart disease
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 240.

questions.question_text: Mrs. Y is an 83-year-old lady whose sister has been diagnosed with early Alzheimer's disease. She is worried that she may develop the same condition. What is her risk compared to a person who lacks such a family history?
questions.explanation: An actual predicted risk of developing Alzheimer's disease in the first-degree relatives of probands with Alzheimer's disease is 15-19%, compared with 5% in controls. Thus, the risk to the first-degree relatives of patients with Alzheimer's disease who developed the disorder at any time up to the age of 85 years is increased some 3 - 4 times relative to the risk in controls (Retrieved from [http://bjp.rcpsych.org/content/178/1/7](https://www.google.com/search?q=http://bjp.rcpsych.org/content/178/1/7)).

questions.question_text: Which of the following can be used as a test of executive functioning in an older person with schizophrenia?
questions.explanation:
A popular test of problem-solving/executive functioning is the Tower of London (or Hanoi) task, which requires subjects to move coloured discs onto three posts to obtain target designs in a set number of moves. It can be used to test frontal lobe function.
Ref: Hodges JR. Cognitive assessment for clinicians, 3rd Edition. 2018. pp. 24, 28-29.

questions.question_text: Ginkgo is a popular herbal remedy for memory enhancement. Patients treated for which of the following conditions should avoid ginkgo?

options.text: Treated for bacterial pharyngitis with amoxicillin
Treated for dental pain with ibuprofen
Treated for atrial fibrillation with warfarin
Treated for Paget disease with alendronate

correct_answer.text: Treated for atrial fibrillation with warfarin

correct_answers.text: Treated for atrial fibrillation with warfarin

questions.explanation:
Several reports have noted that ginkgo may increase the risk of bleeding. The drug is widely used in Germany but less so elsewhere.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 618.

questions.question_text: In dementia with Lewy bodies, visual hallucinations occur in up to
questions.explanation:
Recurrent, complex visual hallucinations occur in up to 80% of patients with dementia with Lewy bodies. They are a frequent clinical signpost to diagnosis. The hallucinations are typically well-formed, featuring people, children, or animals, sometimes accompanied by related phenomena including passage hallucinations, sense of presence, and visual hallucinations.
Ref: McKeith IG et al. Diagnosis and management of dementia with Lewy bodies: Fourth consensus report of the DLB Consortium. Neurology. 2017 Jul 4;89(1):88-100.

questions.question_text: The Hachinski Score is a way of looking into risk factors for
questions.explanation:
The modified Hachinski Ischaemic Score (HIS) is used as a measure of the likelihood of vascular pathology based on the nature of dementia presentation and vascular risk factors. The HIS contains 8 items and scores on the HIS range from 0 to 12: a single point is scored for 4 of the items, with two points scored for each of the remaining 4 items. Clinically a score of greater than 4 on the HIS is indicative of a diagnosis of vascular dementia.
Ref: Titheradge D et al. Cambridge Cognitive Examination and Hachinski Ischemic Score as predictors of MRI confirmed pathology in dementia: A cross-sectional study. International Journal Of Clinical Practice. 2020 Feb;74(2):e13446.

questions.question_text: In Parkinson disease-related psychosis, hallucinations in which sensory modality are the most common?
questions.explanation:
Psychosis in Parkinson disease (PD) is a spectrum of neuropsychiatric manifestations consisting of ‘positive symptoms’, namely illusions, hallucinations, and delusions. Psychosis in PD is often characterised by visual hallucinations. Auditory hallucinations and delusions occur far less frequently, and usually in younger patients. Tactile, olfactory, or somatic hallucinations are quite rare.
Ref: Jones S et al. Neuropsychiatric symptoms in Parkinson's disease: aetiology, diagnosis and treatment. BJPsych Advances. 2020:1-10.
Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 815.
Marinus J et al. Risk factors for non-motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease. The Lancet Neurology. 2018 Jun 1;17(6):559-68.

questions.question_text: In the diagnosis of dementia with Lewy bodies, which of the following is considered a supportive (rather than core) clinical feature?
questions.explanation:
Core clinical features Core clinical features of dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB): of dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB):
●      Fluctuating cognition with pronounced variations in attention and alertness
●      Recurrent visual hallucinations Recurrent visual hallucinations that are typically well formed and detailed
●      REM sleep behaviour disorder REM sleep behaviour disorder, which may precede cognitive decline
●      Spontaneous cardinal features of parkinsonism (bradykinesia, rest tremor, and/or rigidity)
Supportive clinical features of DLB:
●      Severe sensitivity to antipsychotic agents
●      Postural instability
●      Repeated falls
●      Syncope or other transient episodes of unresponsiveness
●      Severe autonomic dysfunction (e.g. constipation, orthostatic hypotension, urinary incontinence)
●      Hypersomnia
●      Hyposmia
●      Systematized delusions
●      Hallucinations in other modalities
●      Apathy, anxiety, and depression
Ref: McKeith IG et al. Diagnosis and management of dementia with Lewy bodies: Fourth consensus report of the DLB Consortium. Neurology. 2017 Jul 4;89(1):88-100.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is classified as a 'behavioural symptom' seen in dementia?
questions.explanation:
Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) occur in over 90% of patients to varying degrees. Behavioural symptoms include aggression, wandering, explosive temper, sexual disinhibition, inappropriate toileting, excessive eating, and searching behaviour.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 644.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 157.
